description:
We're DayBit, six 11th graders from Robert College in Istanbul! We're passionate about entrepreneurship, robotics, badminton, painting, and of course space! 

At NASA Space Apps, we're developing CREWTRACE, a platform helping astronauts make informed health decisions during space missions. We combine engineering, creativity, and curiosity to tackle real-world challenges. 

We'd love to connect with people skilled in coding, biomedical science, data, and design. We're build something awesome!
summary: CREWTRACE helps space crews decide what their health observations actually establish, what to check next, and how to preserve follow-up when ground review is delayed. It connects daily sleep duration, subjective fatigue and resting pulse to a fixed personal reference, checking measurement quality and context before interpreting changes. When evidence is incomplete, its Next-Evidence engine explains which feasible clarification or observation could affect the current finding. Separate onboard and ground endpoints preserve original findings and reconcile corrections after communication interruptions. A Health Atlas and Measurement Coach connect recorded evidence to sourced research, missing information and appropriate collection guidance. NASA terrestrial bed-rest observations provide a real-data demonstration of withholding an unsupported reference. The working prototype addresses astronaut monitoring through an explainable evidence-to-action workflow. Its engineering behavior is tested; improved human decisions and clinical effectiveness remain unestablished. Synthetic mission demonstrations are explicitly labeled
details:
CREWTRACE addresses a practical monitoring problem: a recorded health value may be unsuitable for the question being asked, while the person reviewing it on Earth may not be immediately available. Its intended user is a crew member completing routine check-ins during an exploration mission with interrupted or delayed ground communication.

The application records sleep duration, subjective fatigue and resting pulse, together with time, quality, source and measurement context. It compares eligible observations with a fixed personal median and median absolute deviation. The default reference and change thresholds are explicitly exploratory engineering conventions. Post-exercise or unconfirmed pulse measurements are excluded from resting comparisons, and missing observations never count as reassuring evidence. Concerning symptoms take priority over statistical findings and direct the user toward established mission medical procedures.

The Next-Evidence engine asks which feasible additional check could change a specific software interpretation. It examines bounded joint completions of missing or excluded indicators, shows alternative outcomes, and ranks actions transparently using decision consequences and declared collection costs. Those costs are assumptions, not measured astronaut workload. In the synthetic demonstration, verifying the original rested context of an unchanged 87.7 bpm pulse establishes a second qualifying day and changes the supported finding from watch to persistent. Failed verification leaves the pulse excluded. Missing fatigue remains visible, and stopping a limited comparison never cancels required monitoring or implies medical clearance.

CREWTRACE preserves the original finding, evidence snapshot and follow-up actions. Two independent Node.js endpoints have separate persistent stores and explicit packet exchange. Queues, duplicate-safe receipt, causal ordering and correction reconciliation preserve history through tested interruptions and restarts. Ground receipt, reviewer acknowledgement and follow-up resolution are distinct states. Browser operation supports local persistence and offline use after the application has first been installed online.

The Health Atlas separates observations, published relationships, missing evidence and supported next steps across cardiovascular, renal/hydration and vision/neurological views. It does not invent unavailable organ measurements. Measurement Coach explains collection conditions for the three implemented indicators. Versioned mission-context records can retain activity, headache and declared carbon dioxide observations without asserting exposure causation or flight readiness.

NASA LSDA/NLSP UTMB Campaign 1 actigraphy supplies 207 terrestrial bed-rest records from three volunteers, including 17 missing sleep values. None has enough eligible pre-study observations for the default reference. CREWTRACE therefore withholds that comparison. These observed records remain separate from synthetic mission scenarios.

The release records 226 passing JavaScript checks, five NASA parser/reference checks and 20 successful independent-process scenarios under defined faults. Comparative simulations retain ties and failures: strong simpler policies match CREWTRACE on the main decision-resolution benchmark, and collection-effort differences depend on assumed costs. No human-participant experiment or clinical validation has been conducted.

The implementation uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, browser storage and service workers, Node.js endpoints, and Python analysis. No paid model endpoint is essential. The distinctive contribution is the integration of evidence quality, task-specific collection guidance and inspectable decision continuity. Intended benefits are clearer uncertainty and more coherent follow-up; demonstrating those benefits requires human evaluation. Secure clinical identity, protected health-data storage, validated physiological rules and mission qualification remain future requirements.
